repos.description: Checks whether your README matches your code. Chrome extension + web page for any public JS/TS repo. Rules and five deterministic verifiers decide what's true, Jev labels README lines with calibrated confidence, Haiku explains the findings. Line-linked receipts, status badge, JSON export. Built with AdaL for What Would Jev Do?
repos.readme_head:
# README Clew 2

![README Clew 2: checks whether your README matches your code](web/social-card.png)

Checks whether a GitHub README matches its code.

**Live:** https://readme-clew-2.vercel.app

Paste a public JavaScript or TypeScript repo, press SCAN, and get a claim ledger: every checkable line of the README, what the code says about it, and who decided.

Built for the AdaL "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon, October 6 to 11, 2026.

**Why "clew"?** A clew (said like "clue") is a ball of thread. In the Greek myth, Ariadne gave Theseus a clew so he could follow it back out of the Labyrinth, and it's where the word "clue" comes from. README Clew follows the thread from each README line back to the code. It's also the name of the author's suite of civic tech tools.

---

## What it does

READMEs drift. A command gets renamed, an env var gets dropped, a package gets swapped, and the README keeps promising the old thing. README Clew 2 reads the README line by line and sorts each line into one of four buckets:

| Bucket | Means |
|---|---|
| **Contradicted** | The README says it, the code disagrees. Example: the README tells you to run a start script that `package.json` doesn't have |
| **Missing** | The code does it, the README never mentions it. Example: the code imports a package the README never names |
| **Unverifiable** | No code check can test it (opinions, scope notes, design claims), or Jev wasn't sure what kind of line it was |
| **Verified** | The README and the code agree |

Every row shows the exact README line (with a link to that line on GitHub), the code evidence, and **who decided: a rule or Jev.**

## Screenshots

**A real scan of README Clew v1** (this project's predecessor). No contradictions, four packages the code uses that the README never mentions:

![Report for earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew](assets/screenshots/report.png)

| Home | Key | Phone |
|---|---|---|
| ![Home page before a scan](assets/screenshots/home.png) | ![The KEY tab](assets/screenshots/key.png) | ![A report at phone width](assets/screenshots/phone.png) |

**The Chrome extension popup,** shown with a sample report from the test fixtures (a README that says to run a start script the code doesn't have):

![Extension popup with one Contradicted row](assets/screenshots/extension-popup.png)

## Who it's for

Anyone who maintains or evaluates a JS/TS repo: open source maintainers before a release, hackathon judges reading a submission, and new contributors who want to know which parts of a README they can trust.

## From README Clew to README Clew 2

[README Clew](https://github.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew) (May 2026, Replit Buildathon) proved the idea. Its own README listed two honest limits:

1. Claude was *asked* to quote the README word for word. That was a prompt rule, not a code check.
2. Prose labels like "Frontend (Vite)" sometimes got pulled out as package names, which produced false Contradicted findings.

README Clew 2 is a rebuild from scratch, all new code, that fixes both by changing who decides what:

| Job | README Clew (v1) | README Clew 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Find claims in the README | Claude extracts and quotes | Code splits the README into lines and Jev labels them. The quote *is* the line, so word for word is guaranteed by code |
| Pick the real package, script or path name | Claude | Code finds candidates, Jev picks one, with confidence |
| Decide Verified or Contradicted | Five deterministic verifiers | Same five checks, rewritten. Still fully deterministic |
| Low certainty | Not reported | Goes to Unverifiable, never Contradicted |
| Summary | Claude Sonnet | Claude Haiku, from structured results only |
| Where it runs | Web page | Web page, Chrome extension and bookmarklet |

The demo repo is v1 itself, so the new version audits the old one. Its first scan of v1 was wrong in exactly the way v2 promises not to be, which is how the monorepo fix in "How it was built" happened.

## How it decides (and who doesn't)

The design rule: **models never decide what's true.**

1. **Rules first.** Code splits the README into lines and settles the obvious ones (headings, badges, blank lines) without any model.
2. **Jev labels.** For lines rules can't classify, [Jev](https://typesafe.ai) (TypeSafe's decision model, `jev-1.13.0`, called through [Glasser](https://glasser.ai)) picks what kind of claim the line is: a dependency, a command, an env var, a file or URL, or something no code check covers. Jev only picks labels.
3. **The 0.8 gate.** A line goes to a code check only if Jev is at least 0.8 confident it's one of those four checkable kinds. Below that, it's Unverifiable, tagged "Jev wasn't sure."
4. **Five deterministic verifiers decide.** Dependencies, commands, env vars, file and URL references, and code-vs-package coverage. They read `package.json`, the file tree and the source. Same input, same answer.
5. **Claude Haiku explains.** Haiku writes the short summary from the structured results only (counts, claim types and names). It never sees the README lines themselves and never decides a bucket. If Haiku fails, the report is still complete.

When in doubt, README Clew 2 says "can't tell." Calling a correct README wrong is the one mistake the design works hardest to avoid.

### Where Jev matters

Jev is what lets this work on real READMEs, which are mostly prose. Regex finds candidate names; Jev decides whether a line like "Run the dev server" is a command claim worth checking, and how sure it is. Its calibrated confidence is what the 0.8 gate stands on.

Measured on a held-out set of 32 README lines, frozen configuration, run twice:

| Measure | Run 1 | Run 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong routes passing the 0.8 gate | 0 | 0 |
| False Contradicted (end-to-end scan) | 0 | 0 |
| Real drift found | 3 of 3 | 3 of 3 |

Comparing the two runs, 0 of the 32 lines changed label.

The sample is small, so this supports "safe enough to ship," not a measured error rate. Full numbers and caveats are in [LEDGER.md

# Ghost Rovers **12 machines are still on the Moon and Mars. Only 1 still answers.** A 1969 Mission Control console where kids ages 8 to 12 radio the hardware NASA left behind, on the Moon and on Mars. [**Play it live**](https://earlgreyhot1701d.github.io/ghost-rovers/) · [**Watch the 27-second demo**](https://youtu.be/a_sWWLi5-Xw) · [Slides (PDF)](docs/media/ghost-rovers-slides.pdf) · [**Go to Mars**](https://earlgreyhot1701d.github.io/ghost-rovers/#mars) · [Study notebook](https://notebook.google.com/notebook/c43a9882-26f7-4223-a46c-3f5c332dd378) · [Fact check](docs/FACT_CHECK.md) · [SI disclosure](AI_DISCLOSURE.md) NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · **Abandoned but not Forgotten** · Team **Clew Labs** (La Shara Cordero)
--- ## The problem Kids hear about rockets launching. They almost never hear about what stayed behind. The facts are all in NASA's catalog, but they read like a spec sheet: COSPAR IDs, coordinates, mass budgets. Nobody tells a 9-year-old that a car has been parked on the Moon since before their grandparents had cell phones. ## What Ghost Rovers does You sit at a Mission Control console. Six machines are out there. You pick one and press **CALL GHOST**. Five stay quiet. One answers: the Apollo 11 Laser Mirror. Scientists on Earth still bounce lasers off it, and you watch the beam make the 2.5-second round trip. | The 6 ghosts | Landed | Today | |---|---|---| | Surveyor 3 | Apr 20, 1967 | Quiet since 1967 | | Laser Mirror | Jul 20, 1969 | **Still answers** | | Eagle's Launch Pad | Jul 20, 1969 | Resting since 1969 | | Moonquake Station | Nov 19, 1969 | Switched off 1977 | | Apollo 15 Rover | Jul 30, 1971 | Parked since 1971 | | Apollo 17 Rover | Dec 11, 1972 | Parked since 1972 | Then flip the console to **MARS** (or press M). Six more machines. This time, **none of them answer. Yet.** | The 6 Mars ghosts | Landed | Today | |---|---|---| | Viking 1 Lander | Jul 20, 1976 | Quiet since 1982 | | Viking 2 Lander | Sep 3, 1976 | Batteries failed 1980 | | Sojourner Rover | Jul 4, 1997 | Quiet since 1997 | | Spirit Rover | Jan 4, 2004 | Quiet since 2010 | | Opportunity Rover | Jan 25, 2004 | Quiet since 2018 | | InSight Lander | Nov 26, 2018 | Last heard December 2022 | Kids named some of them. A 12-year-old named Sojourner, and a third grader named Spirit and Opportunity. These 6 are quiet for good, but Mars is not silent. Finish the Mars check and the console points you to the 2 rovers that **still answer** Earth today: Curiosity (Gale Crater, since 2012) and Perseverance (Jezero Crater, since 2021). ## What a kid can do - **Spin the real Moon and Mars.** 3D globes wrapped in NASA maps (the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Moon map and the Viking Mars map), with every landing site marked. - **Call each ghost** and get its reply, with radio static and a 1969 console sound. - **Read its file:** the original mission, a short story in the machine's own voice, and 3 questions kids actually ask ("Could I drive it?" "What's it made of?"). - **See the real photo** big, in a slide viewer, credited by NASA ID. - **Watch the clock.** A live counter shows how long each machine has been on the Moon or Mars, down to the second. - **Tap READ TO ME** to hear the file read aloud. - **Finish all 6** on each world to earn a Junior Flight Controller badge, then keep going with a quiz, flashcards, and a mind map for that world. On Mars, the badge panel also links to Curiosity and Perseverance, the 2 rovers still answering. ## Built on NASA data, checked by a human | Source | Used for | |---|---| | [NSSDCA catalog](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/) | Every date, site, and fact. Each ghost links to its own record | | [NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4720) | LRO color map for the 3D Moon | | [NASA 3D Resources: Mars](https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/mars/) | Viking-based color map for the 3D Mars | | [images.nasa.gov](https://images.nasa.gov/) | 12 photos from the Moon and Mars, resized only | | [NASA JPL](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/the-apollo-experiment-that-keeps-on-giving/) | Laser ranging: still working, Moon drifts 3.8 cm a year | All 12 ghosts were checked line by line against NASA's records. The check caught overclaims and fixed them. Example: "the first car on the Moon" became "the first car astronauts drove on the Moon," because a Soviet robot rover got there first in 1970. Full logs: [Moon](docs/FACT_CHECK.md) · [Mars](docs/FACT_CHECK_MARS.md). ## How it works Plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. No framework, no build step, no server, no login, and no data collected. Two JSON files hold every fact, one per world. Three.js draws the Moon and Mars. | File | Job | |---|---| | `index.html` | The console: clocks, side screens, curved wall screen, desk | | `styles/*.css` | Design tokens plus 10 layout files, one job each (base, screen, plot, console, modals, tablet-landscape, tablet-portrait, phone, phone-compact, rotate-hint), and `still-answering.css` for the Mars still-answering row | | `js/main.js` | State, boot sequence, keys, laser show, clocks, sound, read-aloud | | `js/globe.js` | 3D Moon and Mars, drag to spin, FACE EARTH | | `js/projection.js`, `js/markers.js` | Latitude and longitude to screen pins | | `js/card.js` | Ghost file, answers, photo viewer, badge | | `js/still-answering.js` | Mars only: links to the 2 working rovers that still answer | | `data/ghosts.json`, `data/mars.json` |

repos.description: A typing game, back from the dead. The 80s typing games MasterType and Type Attack, rebuilt as a real trainer for anyone starting or rebuilding keyboard skills. Accuracy-first lessons, a heat map of your missed keys, adaptive drills, and progress saved only in your browser. Built with Kiro for Kiroween 2026.
repos.readme_head:
# Dead Keys

*A typing game, back from the dead.*

> I learned on a typewriter in middle school, and the Mac games at home helped me improve. In 2000, almost half of US high school grads took a typing class. By 2019 it was 2.5%. So I brought the games back.

The number: US high school graduates who earned keyboarding credit fell from 44.1% in 2000 to 2.5% in 2019 ([NCES, NAEP High School Transcript Study, Table 1](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/hsts/2019_tables/2019_table1.aspx)).

**Play it:** [dead-keys.vercel.app](https://dead-keys.vercel.app)

![The Dead Keys title screen: after 3 idle seconds the game plays itself, typing falling words in the outer lanes.](docs/attract.gif)

Dead Keys rebuilds the 1980s typing games MasterType and Type Attack as a keyboard trainer that notices which keys you miss and drills them. Built with [Kiro](https://kiro.dev) for the [Kiroween Hackathon 2026](https://kiroween.devpost.com/), category Resurrection.

## Two resurrections

**MasterType (1981) and Type Attack (1982).** Words fall toward you, and you type them before they land. Dead Keys keeps that pressure and the arcade feel, with synthesized sound and a phosphor-terminal look. It changes what happens after the round: every key you miss is counted, and the game builds the next drill around those keys. No assets from either game are used.

**Office Keys (August 2025).** My first Lovable build, a no-login typing practice app for court staff. Dead Keys keeps its ideas (no accounts, practice the keys that trip you up) and none of its code.

## How to play

1. Press any key on the title screen, or watch the demo play itself.
2. Pick Play, a Daily drill, or a lesson. Choose English or Spanish words on Play.
3. Type each word before it lands. Every key you miss is remembered.
4. After the round, drill the keys you missed, race your own ghost, or share your card.

## How we count

WPM, accuracy and weak keys are explained in the game, on the **How we count** page (from the menu, or the link under your results). Short version: speed is correct characters divided by five, per minute, with pauses left out. Accuracy is right keystrokes over all keystrokes. A miss counts against the key you should have pressed. A personal best only counts at 90% accuracy or better.

## Architecture

```
Browser (static, on Vercel)                    Server (one Vercel function)
  index.html, styles, ES modules                 api/drill.js         POST only, same origin, under 2 KB
  engine/ (pure functions, no DOM)               api/_lib/limits.js   per-visitor limit + daily cap
  ui/ (DOM, textContent only)        POST        api/_lib/prompt.js   weak keys in, prompt out
  storage/ (localStorage, try/catch) ------->    api/_lib/bedrock.js  the only file that talks to AWS
                                     <-------    api/_lib/answer.js   every word checked before it leaves
                       { lines, source } or { error } -> built-in drill
```

The AI writes practice lines from your weak keys with Amazon Nova Micro on Amazon Bedrock. Everything else runs in your browser, and after one visit it installs as an app and plays offline. The service worker (`public/sw.js`) never touches the AI route. If the AI is off, capped, slow or wrong, you get the built-in drill and the game carries on.

**File map.** One file, one job. Source files stay under 150 lines and nothing goes over 250 (a Kiro hook checks).

| Folder | Job |
|---|---|
| `contract/` | The data shapes both halves agree on, and the validator. Frozen after Block 3. |
| `src/engine/` | Rounds, scoring, word timing. Pure functions, no DOM. |
| `src/drills/`, `src/lessons/` | Built-in drills, the daily drill, lessons. |
| `src/ghost/`, `src/attract/`, `src/specwave/` | Ghost race, the title demo, the easter egg. |
| `src/storage/`, `src/packs/` | Local saves and settings; word packs. |
| `src/ui/`, `src/render/`, `src/styles/` | Screens and components; the play field; CSS. |
| `src/sound/`, `src/share/`, `src/analytics/` | Synthesized sound; the share card; page-view counting. |
| `api/` | The AI drill route and its helpers. |
| `packs/` | English and Spanish word packs, their sources and blocklists. |
| `evals/` | The golden set: six weak-key profiles run through the real route. |
| `mcp/` | An MCP server so Kiro can validate packs and run the golden set. |

## Decision records

Short form: context, decision, why, trade-off.

| Decision | Why | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Contract first.** Shapes and fixtures (normal and ugly) before any screen. | Both halves build against the same thing, and a layout that survives the ugly fixtures is ready to wire. | Slower start. Changing a shape later costs a contract change. |
| **Local-only storage.** No accounts, progress in localStorage. | Nothing to breach, nothing to sign up for. | Progress lives in one browser. Backup and import in Settings cover moving it. |
| **Two-layer adaptive drills.** Built-in drills always work; AI drills sit on top. | The game never waits on a model. | Two drill paths to test. |
| **Nova Micro.** Lifecycle Active when checked Nov 7, 2026. | A low-cost Bedrock text model that does the job ($0.035 per 1M input tokens, $0.14 per 1M output, PRD G3). | Other Nova models went legacy in March 2026. Micro could too; the legacy period covers judging, and the fallback covers the rest. |
| **The model's words are checked, not trusted.** Each word must be pack letters, 2 to 12 long, a real English word (SCOWL en_US) and off the blocklist. | The model once wrote "zizz". Nothing it writes reaches you unless it passes. | Some good rare words get dropped too. |
| **Vercel function over Lambda.** | One deploy for site and route. AWS is reached through Vercel OIDC, so there are no AWS keys anywhere. | Tied to Vercel's function runtime. |
| **Vanilla JS with JSDoc.** | No framework to learn or update; types without a build step. | More DOM code by hand. |
| **Synthesized sound.** Web Audio recipes, no audio

repos.description: How far can a 4 GB Chromebook go? A bootstrapping kit built with Claude and GitHub, no IDE and nothing installed: a live app, interactive 3D, an animated diagram, and a demo video, each with real CPU and memory readings. The smallest setup that still keeps a reliable feedback loop. AI assisted. Human approved. Powered by NLP.
repos.readme_head:
# 4 GB and a Dream

**How far can a 4 GB Chromebook go?**

Every build in this repo was made from an HP Chromebook 11a with 4 GB of memory, using [Claude](https://claude.ai) and [GitHub](https://github.com). No IDE. Nothing installed on the laptop. Claude did the building in a cloud workspace and pushed every commit here from the chat.

This is the companion repo for the dev.to article *A Small Laptop Is a Full Build Kit: Bootstrapping with a Chromebook, Claude, and GitHub*. [TODO: link once published]

**Live:** https://earlgreyhot1701d.github.io/4gb-and-a-dream/

## The rounds

| Round | Build | What it shows | Folder |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Necesito](https://github.com/earlgreyhot1701D/necesito) | A live app with no editor | Its own repo |
| 2 | Papel picado, in 3D | Interactive 3D, drawn by the laptop you're on | `round-2-3d/` |
| 3 | The bootstrapping path | An animated diagram of every step, with a "What if the Wi-Fi drops?" button | `round-3-diagram/` |
| 4 | The tour | A 46-second video of every round, recorded and edited in the cloud | `round-4-video/` |

## The kit

| Part | What | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Laptop | HP Chromebook 11a: MediaTek Kompanio 500, 4 GB of memory | Already owned |
| Browser | Chrome | Free |
| Code and hosting | GitHub and GitHub Pages | Free |
| AI that builds | Claude, working in a cloud workspace | Paid plan |

## Round 2: Papel picado, in 3D

Three strings of papel picado flags swaying across a dusk sky, with warm string lights and stars.

- **Drag** or use the **arrow keys** to spin. **Pinch**, **scroll**, or **+ / −** to zoom.
- A **frame-rate meter** in the corner shows how smoothly your device is drawing it.
- It **pauses when the tab is hidden**, so a background tab costs nothing.
- It respects **reduced motion** settings: no swaying if your device asks for less motion.
- One HTML file and one library: [three.js](https://threejs.org) r128, loaded from cdnjs.

Building happened in the cloud. Drawing happens on your device, so this round is the one that makes a small laptop work.

## Round 3: The bootstrapping path

Six steps from a laptop to a live link, colored by where each one runs: on the laptop, in Claude's cloud workspace, or on GitHub. Only two of the six happen on the laptop.

- **Play, pause, or step through** with the buttons. Captions are read aloud by screen readers.
- **What if the Wi-Fi drops?** cuts the laptop's link and shows the cloud steps carrying on without it, like when my Wi-Fi dropped once during the Necesito build.
- A glowing **thread** unspools to the current step, so your eye follows the path. Steps behind it fill in, and steps ahead stay dim.
- Styled in the [Clew Labs](https://clewlabs.org) colors. The thread is the clew.
- Plain HTML, CSS, and a little JavaScript. No libraries.
- Respects **reduced motion**: it starts paused and the moving dashes stay still.

## Round 4: The tour

A 46-second, silent tour of every round. Claude drove a headless browser from a script, recorded it, and encoded it with ffmpeg, all in its cloud workspace. The Chromebook only plays it.

- Recorded from the repo files, the same files GitHub Pages serves, because the cloud workspace can't reach github.io.
- Necesito uses a demo number, and the tap stops at the button. A browser can't film Messages opening.
- The 3D frame-rate meter is hidden in the video, since it would show the recording machine, not the Chromebook.
- The script is `scripts/record_tour.py`. A GIF copy for dev.to is in `assets/article/`.

## Credits

Idea by [Alex Shev](https://dev.to/alexshev), who asked for the bootstrapping path and a capability table.

Built by [L. Cordero](https://dev.to/earlgreyhot1701d) with Claude (Opus 5.5). I directed and decided. Claude wrote the code.

AI assisted. Human approved. Powered by NLP.

MIT License
